item.title: A Primer on Ethics in Mathematics
item.description: arXiv:2610.08209v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This is a course about Ethics in Mathematics. That is, about the ethical issues that arise in mathematics itself, in mathematical work, and in the actions of mathematicians, broadly interpreted to cover all mathematically-powered technologies. This is a novel course. Traditionally, ethics has seldom been considered by, let alone taught within, the mathematics discipline. This course seeks to change that, by bringing to light the specific ethical issues relevant to mathematics, in a way that is clear and understandable to mathematicians. This course is written by mathematicians, for mathematicians, and about mathematicians. It presents new and original material, in the form of case studies covering harmful and unethical behaviour, analysis of the causal chain of events leading to such harm, and examination of the surrounding processes that drive such actions. All this is fully cited, and supported with interactive activities to aid learning. It develops much of the foundational theory of ethics in mathematics: what can go wrong, why it goes wrong, and how to address it. Students and practitioners alike take away an understanding of the context of their mathematical work, and how to change their actions to ensure more appropriate and useful outputs. In contrast to more traditional philosophy teaching, this course does not delve into the depths of ethical theory. Rather, it presents a practical, hands-on, pragmatic approach to ethics in mathematics, treating it as a branch of applied ethics. It uncovers the very particular ethical issues that arise from mathematical technologies, as well as show how general principles from ethics and responsible development apply even to mathematical work. As such, this makes it highly relevant to adjacent areas such as computer science, physics, engineering, and any other numerate discipline.
item.dc:creator: Maurice Chiodo

item.title: Singular Value Decomposition: A Geometric Rediscovery, Where Proofs Become Algorithms
item.description: arXiv:2610.08565v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This article is a geometric rediscovery of the singular value decomposition, with a further claim: the construction it builds is the machinery behind much of machine learning. The same argument that answers an idle question about ellipses is the algorithm behind principal component analysis, kernel methods, and PageRank, and it is not only the results that transfer but the proofs themselves, run as procedures. The usual introduction states $A = U\Sigma V^T$ and justifies it via the spectral theorem applied to $A^T A$. This is correct but unilluminating, since it assumes a powerful theorem to reach a result that is, in the end, about ellipses. Part I reverses the order. A linear map sends the unit circle to an ellipse; one asks which input directions map to its axes, and finds, example after example, that they are perpendicular. In the plane this can be watched: rotate a frame, track how far its images are from perpendicular, and a sign change forces a frame where they are exactly perpendicular, which is also where the map stretches hardest. Maximizing the stretch and recursing generalizes this to n dimensions, with singular values falling out in order, and the construction proves the spectral theorem rather than assuming it. Part II puts each construction to work: maximize-and-recurse becomes the power method and PageRank; the lemma locating the maximizer becomes the stopping rule of gradient descent; the duality between $A^T A$ and $A A^T$ becomes the transport at the heart of kernel PCA. Each connection is stated with its boundary, saying what the decomposition supplies and where another idea takes over. Prerequisites are the standard sophomore sequence, and the worked examples are small enough to check by hand.
